analysis.one_liner: Bars health insurers from denying coverage or setting premiums based on genetic information.
analysis.headline: A bill to stop genetic discrimination in health insurance drew 221 House cosponsors — a majority of the chamber — but never received a committee vote or a floor vote in the two-year Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have prohibited health insurers and group health plans from denying, canceling, or refusing to renew coverage, or changing premiums and terms, based on a person's genetic information or their family members' genetic information, or because someone sought genetic testing or counseling. It also barred insurers from demanding genetic information and required written, per-disclosure authorization before any genetic information could be shared. The protections would have covered employer group plans, individual-market insurance, and Medicare supplement (Medigap) policies, with lawsuits and damages available to enforce them.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone who has taken or might take a genetic test, or whose family carries an inherited disease risk. The bill kept insurers from using that information to deny coverage, charge higher premiums, or drop policies — and protected people's right to learn their own genetic risk without paying for it with their insurance.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits group health plans and insurers from denying, canceling, or refusing to renew coverage, or varying premiums and terms, based on genetic information or on a person requesting or receiving genetic services [S2][S3].
Extends the same ban to insurance sold in the individual market and to Medicare supplemental (Medigap) policies, so protections do not stop at employer plans [S2][S3].

Bars insurers from requesting or requiring genetic information, and requires prior written authorization for each disclosure of it — meaning a person could get tested without the result going into an insurer's underwriting file [S3].
Gives individuals the right to sue for compensatory, consequential, and punitive damages when a plan or insurer violates the ban, instead of leaving enforcement to regulators alone [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and self-insured employer plans, which would lose the ability to use genetic information and family history to screen applicants or price coverage. Insurers argued this could concentrate costs among people who know they are at risk, potentially raising premiums across the pool.

drawbacks.text: The bill would strip insurers of a traditional underwriting tool: with premiums unable to reflect known genetic risk, people who learn they carry a disease risk would be most likely to buy generous coverage, which insurers argue could push premiums up for everyone in the pool. The bill's coverage and premium restrictions are what create this concern [S3].
The private right of action with compensatory, consequential, and punitive damages would add litigation exposure for plans and insurers, a cost that could be passed into premiums [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — letting people learn their genetic risk without losing their health coverage — is substantial, and the United States ultimately adopted similar federal protections in 2008. The main cost is real: barring risk-based pricing can concentrate costs and raise premiums somewhat for the broad pool. On balance, the bill traded a modest, diffuse premium cost for removing a threat that could make genetic testing economically dangerous for individuals.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in its three assigned committees and their subcommittees for the entire two-year Congress — no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote ever happened, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Representative Louise Slaughter introduced the bill on January 6, 1999 [S1][S5].
It was referred to three committees at once — Commerce, Ways and Means, and Education and the Workforce [S5].
Within weeks it went down another layer to subcommittees: Health and Environment and Health under Commerce, and Employer-Employee Relations under Education and the Workforce [S5].
It attracted 221 cosponsors — 189 Democrats, 31 Republicans, and 1 Independent — a majority of the 435-seat House [S4].
After a second set of introductory remarks by the sponsor in May 2000, the record shows no further action; the bill never cleared committee and died at the end of the 106th Congress [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and self-insured employer plans, which kept the ability to deny coverage or price policies using genetic information and family history for years longer.

for.name: Rep. Louise Slaughter
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, spoke for it on the House floor twice, and kept it before the chamber across both years of the Congress.

against.name: House committee leadership
against.role: Chairs of the three committees of referral
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee markup or vote in two years; after subcommittee referral in January 1999, the record shows no committee action of any kind.

against.name: Health insurance industry
against.role: Insurers offering group, individual, and Medigap coverage
against.what_they_did: Opposed legislation restricting the use of genetic information in underwriting, which would have limited insurers' ability to screen applicants and set premiums.

sides.party_line_note: No roll call ever occurred, but support was bipartisan on its face: of 221 cosponsors, 189 were Democrats, 31 were Republicans, and 1 was an Independent [S4].

industries.note: The bill would end insurers' ability to deny, cancel, or re-price coverage based on genetic information — including information about family members — across group, individual, and Medigap markets, and would bar them from even collecting genetic data without authorization [S2][S3]. Insurers' business interest in risk-based underwriting runs directly against the protection customers wanted. The industry's preference for the status quo prevailed because the bill never got a vote.

ERISA plans and the employers behind them would be barred from using genetic information about workers or their families in plan administration [S2][S3]. For employers this removes an underwriting tool but also removes a reason employees might fear employer-sponsored genetic screening.
